name: Aesthefill

lead: AestheFill is a PDLLA microsphere injectable from REGEN Biotech of Seoul, used by clinicians to restore facial volume and, increasingly, body contour. People use it for firmer skin and softer lines that develop gradually.

It contains PDLLA microspheres with carboxymethyl cellulose as a suspending agent, is described as biodegradable and biostimulatory, and prompts tissue to rebuild collagen and volume over time. A randomized, evaluator-blinded multicentre study compared it with hyaluronic acid for nasolabial folds, and much of the other literature concerns reconstitution methods and consensus technique recommendations.

paras: It is supplied as a powder that the clinician reconstitutes with sterile water before injection. Treatment is usually a short series of sessions, with results building over weeks to months.

Technique-related issues such as lumping during reconstitution are discussed in the literature, and specific adverse event rates were not summarised in the sources reviewed. It is administered by trained clinicians.

angle.text: People use AestheFill to firm skin and soften lines like nasolabial folds gradually. The PDLLA microspheres stimulate collagen so tissue rebuilds over time. A randomized trial compared it with hyaluronic acid for nasolabial folds.

lead: AestheFill is an injectable poly-D,L-lactic acid (PDLLA) microsphere product made by REGEN Biotech of Seoul, South Korea. It is a biostimulator: instead of only adding volume itself, it is injected into or under the skin to prompt the body to build collagen and soft tissue over the following weeks. People use it to soften nasolabial folds, fill hollows under the eyes, improve skin texture and, increasingly, rejuvenate areas of the body.[1][2][3]

The product contains PDLLA microspheres with carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) as a suspending agent, supplied as a lyophilised powder that the clinician reconstitutes with sterile water before injection. It is described as biocompatible, biodegradable and biostimulatory.[1][3] The thickness of the suspension can be varied for different targets, from nose or chin augmentation to skin rejuvenation.[4]

A randomised, evaluator-blinded multicentre study compared it with hyaluronic acid for nasolabial fold augmentation in 260 patients.[1] Much of the remaining literature concerns reconstitution methods and consensus technique recommendations from clinician groups.[2][3][5][6]

paras: AestheFill is one of several polylactic acid injectables. Polylactic acid comes as poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) and poly(D,L-lactic acid) (PDLLA), which differ in stereoisomeric structure; both are used as dermal fillers for soft tissue augmentation.[7] In AestheFill the microspheres do not dissolve in water, while CMC acts as a suspender; the powder is agglomerated into granules to limit CMC lumps during reconstitution.[3]

Practitioners adjust how much water is added to change the suspension. One group of injectors described four tiers, from the thickest suspension for nose or chin augmentation, through thick for deep wrinkles and thin for shallow wrinkles, to a super-thin form for skin rejuvenation.[4] It can also be used for skin texture improvement through intradermal injection with an automatic multi-needle injector.[6]

Wikipedia describes polylactic acid fillers as acting differently from hyaluronic acid fillers, which give immediate volume. Instead the particles break down and the body's response, which involves macrophages and fibroblasts, produces new collagen and fibrous tissue.[8] Because the effect builds over time, injectors often plan treatment in stages. Fillers in general are regulated as medical devices, and in the US a provider must perform the injection.[8]

A paper from Taiwan proposed a simple PDLLA injection method for the lower eyelid in Asian patients with tear trough deformities, infra-orbital hollows, nasojugal grooves, dark eye circles or mild eye bags. The authors reported injecting more than 100 patients since 2019 with high satisfaction and only mild, transient swelling, redness and bruising.[9]

Demand for non-surgical body rejuvenation has grown, and an AestheBody guide describes use on the neck, chest, abdomen, buttocks, arms, thighs, knees and hands, noting that large surfaces need more product and careful planning.[10][11]

A large share of AestheFill publications concern preparation. Six reconstitution methods have been summarised, with hydration of the granules and dispersion of the CMC and PDLLA particles identified as the two time-consuming steps.[3] Papers also compare reconstitution of AestheFill with Sculptra,[5] and describe a warm-water soak with back-and-forth mixing intended to eliminate micro-aggregates and stop needle clogging.[6]

Brazilian experts used a modified Delphi method to draft consensus recommendations on reconstitution, injection technique and patient management for facial and non-facial treatments.[2] The AestheCode system, proposed by clinicians with about ten years of experience, links suspension thickness, injection layer and method to each indication; the authors note that biostimulators tend to form non-inflammatory nodules if technical mishaps occur.[4] A 2025 laboratory comparison found AestheFill and NeoFilera had similar functional groups, size distribution, osmotic pressure and viscosity, whereas Sculptra differed in particle shape and viscosity.[7]

A randomised, evaluator-blinded, multicentre study published in Aesthetic Surgery Journal in 2024 compared injectable PDLLA (AestheFill) with hyaluronic acid for nasolabial fold augmentation, noting that its efficacy and safety had not previously been studied in a large cohort. Two hundred and sixty patients with moderate to severe folds were randomised and followed for 52 weeks using the Wrinkle Severity Rating Scale and the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale. At 24 weeks, 67.6% of the PDLLA group had at least a 1-grade WSRS improvement, compared with 60.9% of the hyaluronic acid group.[1]

The lower eyelid case series reported high satisfaction among more than 100 treated patients,[9] and the Brazilian consensus draws on practitioner experience rather than a controlled trial.[2] Authors of the technique papers assign them low levels of evidence under the journal scale.[4][11]

Authors of the lower eyelid series reported mild, transient swelling, redness and bruising.[9] Biostimulator injection errors are associated with non-inflammatory nodules, which the AestheCode paper aims to prevent through choice of layer and suspension.[4] Wikipedia lists bruising, redness, pain and itching among common effects of improperly performed filler procedures, and notes that infection or allergic reaction can occasionally cause lumps that need correction.[8]

AestheFill is marketed globally by REGEN Biotech[2] and is discussed mainly in clinician literature and aesthetic practice. Clinical training material such as the AestheCode and AestheBody guides, written by users of the product, shapes how it is injected.[4][10]
